sources.title: Allan Adams, Nima Arkani-Hamed, Sergei Dubovsky, Alberto Nicolis, and Riccardo Rattazzi, Causality, Analyticity and an IR Obstruction to UV Completion
sources.locator: Section 4, PDF pp. 14–20, equations (21)–(24) and (30)–(34): forward contour, paired poles/cuts, high-energy closure, optical-theorem weight, and the mass-gap/IR caveat.

contents.name: Section 4 forward contour and optical-theorem moment

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete relevant forward-contour passage in PDF pp. 14–20, including the residue evaluation, paired cuts, outer contour, and optical-theorem relation.
source_review.supports: In a specified scalar model with analytic forward amplitude, crossing, a controlled high-energy arc, and nonnegative cross section, the forward low-energy coefficient is constrained by a positive spectral integral.
source_review.limitations: The source develops its stated scalar/IR-regulated cases; it does not give a universal sign for every off-shell coefficient or extend the proof through massless forward poles/cuts.

contents.name: Mass gap, stable-pole subtraction, and massless-cut caveat

source_review.read_extent: Read the analytic-structure and IR-regulation discussion in PDF pp. 14–20.
source_review.supports: A positive mass gap moves pair-production cuts away from the subtraction point; stable poles and massless exchange require explicit treatment.
source_review.limitations: The local definition adopts a gapped amplitude package and makes no massless-channel conclusion.

contents.name: Use in the coefficient comparison

source_review.read_extent: The same complete Section 4 forward argument was inspected.
source_review.supports: The example applies only the necessary forward-coefficient sign under the same fixed assumptions.
source_review.limitations: The source does not assert that a coefficient passing one inequality is sufficient for a full amplitude.

sources.title: Claudia de Rham, Scott Melville, Andrew J. Tolley, and Shuang-Yong Zhou, Positivity Bounds for Scalar Theories
sources.locator: Complete five-page paper; §§2.1–2.2, equations (1)–(15), PDF pp. 1–3: partial-wave convention, two-subtraction dispersion relation, crossing, pole subtraction, and positive forward derivatives.

contents.name: Equations (1)–(4): partial waves and forward absorptive sign

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete partial-wave/optical-theorem and analyticity discussion in §§2.1–2.2, PDF pp. 1–3.
source_review.supports: The stated scalar partial-wave normalization and unitarity imply a nonnegative forward absorptive part under the paper assumptions.
source_review.limitations: The authored channel records the sign as a conditional input and does not derive a physical Hilbert-space representation.

contents.name: Equations (5)–(15): crossing-even pole-subtracted dispersion moments

source_review.read_extent: Read the full relevant derivation through the two-subtraction representation and positive moments in §§2.1–2.2.
source_review.supports: A gapped scalar forward coefficient is expressed through a positive dispersive integral after crossing and pole subtraction.
source_review.limitations: The source assumptions are not a theorem about arbitrary massless gauge/gravity channels; the local theorem states its own precise conditional hypotheses.

contents.name: Application to a selected EFT coefficient

source_review.read_extent: Read the low-energy EFT matching discussion following equations (12)–(15).
source_review.supports: The derivative of the pole-subtracted amplitude is matched to low-energy EFT data and can constrain coefficient combinations.
source_review.limitations: The numerical candidate values in the local example are calculated locally and are not source-reported.

sources.title: Ivano Basile, Luca Buoninfante, Francesco Di Filippo, Benjamin Knorr, Alessia Platania, and Anna Tokareva, Lectures in Quantum Gravity
sources.locator: Complete 303-page lecture-notes PDF retrieved; §§3.2.1–3.3.1, printed pp. 90–98: analyticity, partial waves, Martin–Froissart growth, and the simplest forward positivity bound.

contents.name: Section 3.2.1: analytic continuation, cuts, and mass-gap domain

source_review.read_extent: Read §3.2.1, printed pp. 90–91, including the fixed-transfer analytic domain and the massless-cut caveat.
source_review.supports: The notes distinguish physical real kinematics from analytic continuation and identify the role of a mass gap and threshold cuts.
source_review.limitations: The local item states analyticity as input; it does not derive it from a causality axiom.

contents.name: Sections 3.2.2–3.2.3: partial-wave unitarity and high-energy growth

source_review.read_extent: Read §§3.2.2–3.2.3, printed pp. 91–94, including the optical-theorem relation and Froissart bound assumptions.
source_review.supports: Unitarity yields a positive forward absorptive contribution, and mass-gap analyticity with polynomial boundedness controls high-energy growth.
source_review.limitations: The physical channel records the stricter uniform o(|v|^2) and convergence assumptions directly rather than inferring them from a finite EFT.

contents.name: Section 3.3.1: simplest forward positivity bound

source_review.read_extent: Read §3.3.1, printed pp. 96–98, including contour deformation, discontinuities, the optical theorem, and the low-energy second derivative.
source_review.supports: The forward coefficient sign follows from analytic continuation, a mass gap, controlled growth, crossing, and a positive absorptive part.
source_review.limitations: The PDF identifies itself as a lecture-notes submission and has blank publication fields; it is used as a complete lecture treatment, not represented as a final published book.

contents.name: One-inequality example scope

source_review.supports: The necessary sign test can exclude a negative matched coefficient when the exact EFT-to-amplitude map has zero remainder.
source_review.limitations: Passing the inequality is not an existence or sufficiency result.

sources.title: C. P. Burgess, Introduction to Effective Field Theory
sources.locator: Full 55-page review PDF retrieved; §§2.2.1, 2.2.3–2.2.4, and the opening of §2.2.5, printed pp. 20–25: Wilson action and model-specific matching.

contents.name: §2.2.1: Wilson action from high/low mode integration

source_review.read_extent: Read §2.2.1, printed pp. 20–21, including the split of high and low modes and the Wilson-action definition.
source_review.supports: An EFT matching prescription is tied to a declared mode split and a selected low-energy action.
source_review.limitations: The local scalar amplitude is supplied as separate physical data; this review does not construct its S-matrix.

contents.name: §§2.2.3–2.2.4: matching observables and tree-level low-energy action

source_review.read_extent: Read the matching prescription in §2.2.3 and the complete tree-level calculation in §2.2.4, printed pp. 23–25.
source_review.supports: Matching equates selected low-energy observables in full and effective descriptions; tree-level Wilson coefficients are model- and truncation-dependent.
source_review.limitations: The local theorem treats its exact coefficient identity as an explicit input and makes no generic matching theorem claim.

contents.name: Higher-order and one-loop matching context
contents.reason: The local theorem retains only the exact matched v^2 identity; no one-loop coefficient or general Wilson-action construction is imported.
